aio_response.text:
When the Federal Reserve increases interest rates, it raises borrowing costs across the economy, which cools overall demand and helps bring down high inflation .

How Rate Hikes Lower Inflation

• Higher Borrowing Costs: The Fed raises the federal funds rate (the benchmark overnight bank lending rate), which pushes up prime rates, credit card APRs, auto loans, and mortgages.
• Reduced Spending and Demand: More expensive credit discourages households and businesses from taking out loans for major purchases, housing, or business expansions. As demand for goods and services drops, upward pressure on prices and wages eases.
• Encouraged Saving: Higher rates increase yields on savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), and money market funds, prompting consumers to save more and spend less.

Limitations and Side Effects

• Economic Lags: The impact of rate changes does not happen overnight. It typically takes time for tighter financial conditions to ripple through the entire economy, meaning the Fed must project future trends rather than react solely to past data.
• Uneven Sector Impact: Rate-sensitive industries—such as housing and auto manufacturing—tend to absorb the brunt of the slowdown, whereas service-sector inflation can remain sticky and persistent.
• Broader Risks: Aggressive tightening can slow economic growth, raise the unemployment rate, increase debt servicing burdens, and strain the financial or banking sectors.

For more details on how monetary policy interacts with prices, see the Federal Reserve FAQ on Inflation and Employment and Investopedia's Guide on Inflation and Interest Rates .
